title: Yayati and the seasons of a life
hook: Yayati borrows his son's youth and learns that each aim of life has its season.
carry: each aim of life has its season
tomorrow: a book about desire draws its own family tree. who's in it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri met fate with effort: fate is real, and effort is still the means. Today the week closes on a king who wouldn't let his season end.

King Yayati, in the Mahabharata, is cursed with old age too soon. He may pass it to one of his sons, if one will take it. Only the youngest, Puru, agrees, and gives his father his youth. For a thousand years, the story says, Yayati enjoys every pleasure. Then he gives the youth back. Desire, he says, is never quenched by enjoying it; it only grows, like a fire fed with ghee. He crowns Puru and goes to the forest.
screen: `OLD AGE, TOO SOON.` → `A SON GIVES HIS YOUTH.` → `A FIRE FED WITH GHEE.`

segments.voice: Hindu teaching gives the aims of life seasons, and the ashramas, the stages of life, carry them: the student, the householder, the one who steps back, the one who renounces. The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter gives its own version. In childhood, learning. In youth and the middle years, artha and kama, a living and love. In old age, dharma, and the search for moksha, release. The aims take turns, so none crowds out the rest. Yayati tried to stretch one season forever, and found the fire only grew. Then the chapter admits a catch: life is uncertain, so a person may practice each aim as its moment comes, not only on schedule. One thing it won't bend on: the years of study come first. Now hold up the week. Arjuna answering the cry at the gate. Ravana letting one aim swallow the rest. A butcher teaching a scholar the dharma for all. Kama burned, and still a rightful aim. Kichaka turning the order upside down. Savitri meeting fate with effort. Two very different books, and the old stories around them, working on one question: how dharma, artha, kama and moksha share one human life.
screen: `THE ASHRAMAS: SEASONS OF A LIFE.` · `LEARNING, LOVE AND LIVING, THEN DHARMA.` · `YAYATI: DESIRE FED ONLY GROWS.` · `NOW HOLD UP THE WEEK.` · then, large: `EACH AIM HAS A SEASON.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable. On each slow breath, let one season of your own life come to mind, one past, the one you're in, one still ahead, and simply notice which aim has filled it. Rest on the season you're in for the last few breaths. If you pray, close by saying a name of God you love, once. If you don't, close with a quiet thank you for this season.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: the aims in seasons, learning, then a living and love, then dharma and moksha, each in its moment.
screen: `THE KAMA SUTRA'S ETHICS CHAPTER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each aim of life has its season. Yayati found the fire only grows. That's a week.

howItsDone: Hindu teaching often pairs the aims of life with the ashramas, the stages of life, from student to householder to later years of stepping back; the Kama Sutra's opening gives its own version, and Yayati's story is the classic warning against clinging to one season.

fork.reveal: the chapter gives old age to dharma and the search for moksha, and Yayati found desire fed only grows. and since life is uncertain, 'later' is the riskiest plan of all.
